utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could get help with the blind. How did you say you pronounce the witness's surname, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the correct pronunciation of the witness's surname is "Vole."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Vole.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Vole, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask him to say it slowly when you introduce him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm told it's an old Norse term that means "wall" or "fortification."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wall not war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. Just wear your headphones and then make the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm hearing French, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you hear something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Hvaal will be testifying here today pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Morten Hvaal?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you a citizen of Norway?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: I'm a photographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in March 1995?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And two days ago in my office, did you have an opportunity to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does that statement accurately reflect your declaration and what you would say if examined orally today?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would seek to tender what is 65 ter number 9360, which is the ICTY statement of this witness from 28 March 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 9360 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P376, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hvaal, do you recall giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in February of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, on Saturday, did you have an opportunity to review that statement in my office?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does that statement accurately reflect your declaration and what you would say if examined orally today?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would seek to tender what is 65 ter number 9361, which is a redacted version of Mr. Hvaal's statement from February 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P377, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hvaal, do you recall giving testimony before this Tribunal in the trial of Stanislav Galic on the 24th and 25th January 2002?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And two days ago, did you have the opportunity to review the transcript of your testimony in my office?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does that testimony transcript accurately reflect your declaration and what you would say if examined orally today?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would submit 65 ter numbers 9363, which is redacted version of Mr. Hvaal's testimony from 24 January 2002; and 65 ter 9364, which is a redacted version of Mr. Hvaal's testimony from 25 January 2002; and associated exhibits 65 ter 2998, 3000, and 3007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 9363 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P378 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then you have 65 ter 9364, 2998, 3 000, and 3007. May they be admitted into evidence and given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 09364 will be Exhibit P379; 65 ter 02998 will be Exhibit P380; 65 ter 03000 will be Exhibit P381; and 65 ter 03007 will be Exhibit P382, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, I will now give a summary of the evidence that has just been tendered for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Morten Hvaal is a photojournalist who has reported for many conflict zones around the world. Between 1992 and 1997, Mr. Hvaal was based in Sarajevo where he worked for the Associated Press news agency. Between 1992 and 1995, Mr. Hvaal observed positions controlled by the Bosnian/Serb army, as well as areas controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Hvaal witnessed a number of sniping and shelling incidents in Sarajevo where civilians were killed or wounded. Mr. Hvaal also arrived on the scene of sniping and shelling incidents shortly after they occurred. In addition, Mr. Hvaal and his colleagues were also targets of snipers as they drove through the streets of Sarajevo. Mr. Hvaal photographed these incidents and other aspects of life in Sarajevo for the Associated Press. Your Honours, may I have your permission to ask several more questions of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hvaal, you and I speak the same language so we need to be careful to pause at the end of questions and answers to let the interpreters catch up, all right? From when to when did you work in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: From April of 1992 until 1995 as photographer; and then from there on, for another two years or slightly less than two years as an operations manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who were you working for at that time?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: I worked for the Associated Press.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 1992, was the Associated Press a small news agency, medium, or large?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: The Associated Press is the world's largest and oldest news gathering organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was that also true in 1992 and the subsequent years?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind of events did you photograph in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: I was part of the team that covered as many aspects of the conflict and the situation in the whole of the former Yugoslavia, and I was then the team member that was -- who was in Sarajevo. We tried to cover anything that we found to be relevant to the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And can you give a few examples, please?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Obviously, the results of acts of war are and will be the focus of any journalism that takes place in a conflict area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. After you took your photographs, how would they be disseminated by the Associated Press?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: The Associated Press photography and text television and news service functions on a subscription basis; meaning that a large number of media outlets throughout the world receive a service of photographs, text, television, and radio news. The photographs that we would take on assignment would be transmitted to our headquarters in London, and from there on distributed to our network or the Associated Press network all over the world, to clients all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, were your photographs from Sarajevo published in the news media?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes. We closely monitor to what extent our production is published.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, what kind or kinds of news media published your photos from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: The Associated Press is one of the leading agencies obviously; and in most cases, if a newspaper or a magazine has one or two -- subscribes to one or two news agencies, the Associated Press will be one of them. So it's fair, I think, to say that on an important story like the situation in Sarajevo during those years, most major international media would at some point have used the production that we transmitted out from there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind or kinds of media are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: I'm talking about major international newspapers, magazines, television channels that sometimes use still photographs, as well as, you know, this -- it's a broad service. It goes out to anyone basically. There's also the possibility of buying this directly from the files of the AP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know how many media outlets published your photos from Sarajevo? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: You mean throughout the period?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: It would be in the thousands and thousands. I mean, the Associated Press photo service reaches several thousands newspapers every day. So many of them would have used photographs from Bosnia and from Sarajevo on a fairly regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we please show the witness -- it's actually now part of Exhibit -- excuse me, it is now Exhibit P380. Can we please show the witness that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hvaal, do you recognize this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you take it?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where and when was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: This photograph was taken, I believe, in August of 1993, in what we referred to as the French hospital in Sarajevo. It is a photograph of a, I believe, five-year-old girl by the name of Irma Hadzimuratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And she appears to have some bandages on her abdominal area. Do you know what caused her injuries?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: She was wounded in a mortar attack that also killed her mother, and I believe in the backyard of the building where she lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was this photograph disseminated by the Associated Press to its media subscribers?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: It was part of the media coverage of this incident that led to the first proper evacuation of wounded children from Sarajevo since the beginning of the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who carried out that evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: The first evacuation was of Irma herself and her father, as I recall. That was carried out by the royal air force, the British royal air force. Later on, several or many other children were flown out. I believe the first two aeroplanes that came in were Hercules planes from Britain and Sweden. Those were the first planes that came in to evacuate these children, but this went on over a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was the Associated Press the only news agency to cover the story about this girl named Irma?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: No. As a result of this initial photograph, the other media obviously caught on to this story, and I think it became the -- for quite sometime, you know, it was the main story out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "the other media," are you talking about local media or international media or a mix?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: In this particular case, everyone, but particularly the international media, television, news agencies, other photography agencies, newspapers. Basically, all the international media and I suspect most of the national media that were in Sarajevo at the time would have covered this in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before I hand you over, Mr. Hvaal, you mentioned that you started working as a photographer and later as an operations manager.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did your work entail as an operations manager.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was responsible for the well-being of the Associated Press staff, both international and local, throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you were no longer running around and photographing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of the Dayton agreement when hostilities effectively ceased, it was decided that I would be more useful given my experience in the area trying to assist a large of number of staff that came in following the international troops that moved in to Bosnia shortly after that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In what way did you assist this large number of staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By providing -- by making sure that they had the equipment they needed, such as armoured vehicles, personal safety equipment; that everyone had the training they needed; and other equipment that they would need to survive and operate in these fairly hostile conditions. I also made sure that they had the communications equipment, such as satellite communications equipment and so on, to function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So going back to my question, you at that time were no longer going about taking photographs of incidents that were happening. It was the other people who were doing that. You were doing -- you were making sure that you give them logistical support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, when you were now a operations manager.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Effectively, when I became operations manager, obviously, I still have my cameras with me. If there was an incidents, I would photograph it. I didn't cease to be a photographer. But my main responsibility as of sometime 1995, after the siege of Sarajevo began to lift and it was no longer that critically difficult to work there, I -- my responsibility was shifted, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, I guess you are the one coming out, coming forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just prepare after having taken up a reserve position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hvaal, good evening. Did I pronounce your name right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Not bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm Novak Lukic, and on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Perisic, I'm going to put a few questions to you now. In fact, when you were answering Mr. Saxon's questions, you already covered part of the first topic that I wanted to deal with, and it has to do with certain specific matters in relation to a news agency and other media. As far as I know, as a layperson, the difference between a news agency and other media television and other media that cover what is known as reporting, is that an agency carries news in effect, does not make comments. It is an agency's job to convey a certain piece of information, a piece of news, and then hands it over to other media that then further disseminate it; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Not quite, no. Larger news organisations also produce journalism back in the shape of commentary and so on, opinion pieces and so on. So it's a very broad service. It basically covers pretty much everything you need to run national or international coverage in a newspaper. Certainly, in a combination of agencies, you would be able to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, what I see is that, in essence, a news agency receives information and then it is supposed to convey this information further to someone who wants to present it through the media to the public. The essence of an agency's work is that they do not provide comments of their own; for example, like editorials or commentaries in TV studios, things like that. A news agency only deals with news and tries to sell it further on, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Again not quite, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Hasn't Mr. Lukic merely repeated his last question which was already answered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought I wasn't repeating my question, but if it seems that I did repeat my question, I was just trying to be more specific. It seems that my questions are too extensive and too confused, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A news agency, does it provide information directly to the end user; that is, to say, the public?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes. Today it does in the form of electronic news certainly. In those days, this was before the internet, it still provided news coverage directly to the public in the form of radio transmissions, for instance. So it is a finished product that leaves the news agency. These are not -- it's not just a stream of information. It is a finished product, finished stories, finished photographs, finished television reproductions, and so on. Also, as you asked earlier, this is also something that is sold; people subscribe to this. So they've already paid; you don't sell individual stories. People have already paid through a service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do they still pay for the service even today when you are accessible through internet? So the end user can go straight to the internet and get the information from you, instead of getting it via another media who has got it from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are a number of different ways of doing this. The large international news agencies, like the Associated Press, Reuters, AFPDA, and so on, still operate on a subscription basis. The smaller agencies do individual sales on behalf of individual photographers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what I manage to see from your statements and from your testimony, generally speaking, you were in the territory the former Yugoslavia; that's the term that we use here. Even that -- you were there even before you came to Sarajevo in 1992. When was it that you first worked at Associated Press office anywhere in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: That would have been in early 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So from early 1991 onwards, before you went to the territory of Sarajevo, for the most part, you were in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Well, Sarajevo is also in the former Yugoslavia, so I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1991, up until you went to Sarajevo for a longer stint in April 1992, did you spend the interim period in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Not all of it, no. I was there -- I was based in Belgrade for a few months in 1991, and then I left and did several other stories in other parts of the world before coming back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, during 1991, you also covered the territory of Eastern Slavonia and the war in Croatia, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Associated Press office in Belgrade was actually in Belgrade during the times of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, pre-war Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period while you were in Belgrade. While you were still in Belgrade before you went to Sarajevo, did you have occasion to follow the reporting of the Yugoslav media, the Belgrade media; or did you hear the comments of those media about reporting from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: To some extent, yes. But a photographer spends most of his day either in the field or in those days in a dark room, so you try and focus on the information that is necessary in order for you to provide -- or in order for me as a photographer to provide the coverage and the photography that I need to do. So there isn't a lot of time left for perusing local newspapers and having them translated and so on, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, at the time, were you aware of the opinion that prevailed that the authorities were heavily influencing the media, especially the state-owned media and TV, anywhere in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Like most places in the world, I suspect, with the exception of a very limited number of countries, there is going to be some degree of government interference in media. To what extent that was taking place in the former Yugoslavia and with the Belgrade based media, would be very difficult for me to give an exact analysis of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo, did you have occasion to follow the reporting of their media? Although I assume that you do not understand the B/C/S language very well, did you have interpreters or translators, and did you know what their reporting about events was like?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Our field office in Sarajevo had a number of translators and local journalists working for it whose job it was to follow the news coverage. Because of the technical difficulties of producing printed news coverage in a city under siege with no water, no electricity, and so on, basically most of this was limited to listening to radio transmissions when there was electricity to power these radio stations. We would listen to, with our translators, the radio transmissions from all sides, any radio station that we could listen to. That would include all parties to the conflict at that time. Now, some of these stations were established and operated over a long periods of time, others came and went depending on their access to the technical resources that were necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the Oslobodjenje newspaper in Sarajevo, a daily newspaper in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes. It would be very hard not to notice the Oslobodjenje building when you drive past it every day for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was a TV programme broadcast when there were power cuts? Was there any television in Sarajevo actually?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Watching television was not a priority for us given that we had to run generators to do so. Most people didn't even have generators. So I can't say that I watched a lot of television of any sorts, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you said to me a few moments ago that you tried to listen to radio broadcasts containing information coming from all sides, would you agree with me that information, regardless of the media that you followed them through, that the party that was providing the information never spoke of the crimes committed by their own people, their own side, if you will, and that that was a rule in terms of reporting in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: No, I can't be that categorical. I haven't listened to enough of it to say that, so I can't be that categorical, no. I'm not aware of whether or not there has been reports of incidents that were referred to as crimes. In fact, there was a period of time in Sarajevo when there were gang wars going on, and I know that that was to some extent reported, and that would involve reporting on criminal acts obviously. So no, I don't think you can, say, give a blanket statement that there was no reporting like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there were situations in the media when the side on which the victims were would intentionally focus on crimes -- on these crimes, saying that they were committed by the other side actually, even if they weren't?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: You mean, are you asking about whether or not there are specific incidents of misrepresentation of criminal acts? There's a -- no, I can't give you any specific examples. I can say that there is obviously, in all conflicts, a great degree of -- or a great lack of accuracy in all reporting. There's an a element of propaganda in all reporting. But whether this included direct misrepresentation of crimes reported by the local media, no, I couldn't tell you that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in Sarajevo in February 1994 when the incident at Markale occurred?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: No, I was not there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps in Belgrade at the time?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to move on to another topic, some basic postulates pertaining to news reporting. Can you give me a brief answer as to whether you agree with me that a journalist that is conveying agency news first and foremost has the task of providing objective information to the public?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: To the extent that that is possible, yes. It's a matter of building the largest and most accurate report as possible, and this usually is done by using many sources and many points of reference. For instance, no story would ever leave Sarajevo without having been seen by the Belgrade bureau. So it's not a matter of one person writing a story in one place and then presenting that as an objective truth. It's always a large team involved in reporting for a large news agency on a -- in an important story like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the task of every journalist, when he wants to send some information, to check with as many sources as possible the veracity of that information and that he or she believes in the truthfulness of that information?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me - and I think that we heard that from your previous answer when you were giving answers to the Prosecutor in relation to the photograph that we were looking at - that journalists have a greet influence over the creation of public opinion?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Sometimes, no, not necessarily always. The -- leading up to that particular photograph, I must have photographed dozens of equally tragically wounded children in Sarajevo hospitals, and this coverage had resulted in absolutely no response from the other media or the public or the international community as all. So it's not always the case. It depends on many factors and some are still a complete mystery to me as to why one photograph will make a difference and another one will not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate, I concluded on the basis of your testimony that through the media this photograph caused quite a reaction, or at any rate, yielded the effect of having children treated abroad, so in a way it is that photograph that galvanized the public, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: I would say that initially it galvanized the media, and then from there on pressure was brought on in a number of western countries. And I think the country that responded most quickly to that was Britain. Now, whether or not the British government reacted as a result of the situation itself or as a result of pressure from the media, that you would have to ask the British government about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that images concerning the suffering of children and stories about the suffering of children have the greatest impact in the public -- on the public, and generally speaking anything that has to do with children?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. No. That would be far too simplistic to put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said to me a few moments ago that you took quite a few pictures of children in the Sarajevo hospital and that you sent these photographs through your agency, I assume, to the headquarters of your agency?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you send the pictures of two dead children that you took when you were viewing the positions of the Serb side in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: The story of the two children in the morgue there was a bit difficult because we had no way of checking what the background for this story was. I don't believe that those photographs were transmitted simply because we didn't have what was regarded as accurate information on that. We had no means of checking with any independent source on that. We were only given information by either military personnel or the personnel -- people who worked at the hospital or in the morgue as far as I recall. I can't give you a hundred percent accurate answer on who gave us that information, but we were not -- we didn't have any information from, for instance, the children's parents or relatives or neighbours or anybody who could tell us what had happened. So it was an indirect source to this, which means that I don't recall whether or not the photographs of those two children were transmitted. I do recall that the same children were shown to us every time we drove through there, but whether or not they were transmitted, I can't tell you, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the persons who showed you the photographs told you? How was it that these children had lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: No, I don't recall the -- the exact cause of death for them, no. They had -- no, it would be speculation. I can't tell you exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you had no means of checking the sources, I'll move on to another subject though. Do you remember about an incident, was the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992 when there was a problem of providing oxygen for newborn babies in the Banja Luka hospital from Belgrade? This was present throughout the media, that was a problem because the oxygen couldn't be taken to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: I may have heard of it, but I don't remember any details about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know whether anyone from your agency went to Banja Luka to verify this information?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. By the sound of it, I would assume I was not in Belgrade at the time because I'm fairly certain I would have remembered something like that if I had been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to move on to another topic now, so then perhaps I could steal three minutes of our time today and finish early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may do so if you want to finish early.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I don't think it would be a good idea for me to move on to a new topic now, so perhaps I should stop at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. We will then stand adjourned to tomorrow. If you could come back here, sir, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Let me warn you - and I'm sure you know of this, you've testified here, I'm sure, more than once - that you are not allowed to discuss the case with anybody now that you've taken the witness stand. We'll see you tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Court is adjourned to tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of December 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m. to
